newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 8.

text.p: THE DOMINION

The father of the New Zealand victim in Tasmania's Port Arthur massacre said on Thursday his son's killer should be locked up for the rest of his life. Martin Bryant, 29, laughed as he pleaded guilty on Thursday to all 35 murders, reversing an earlier plea of not guilty. Page 1.

Influential NZ First MP John Delamere indicated on Thursday National would have to agree to scrap the $1 billion cap on Maori Treaty settlements to win favour with Maori MPs in NZ First. Delamere, who is a senior figure within NZ First, said

any deal with either party would have to be taken back to respective party caucuses for final approval. He said the biggest issue for Maori in relation to National was the $1 billion cap on the fiscal envelope. NZ First's policy is no cap, as is Labour's. Page 1.

The Dairy Board is battling "an unexpected and astounding" challenge from Britain over exports to the European Union of spreadable butter, worth $45 million a year. Spokesman Neville Martin said the challenge had come from British Customs and Excise officials. They argued the manufacturing method -- which

differed from that of ordinary butter -- did not meet the manufacturing definition laid down in New Zealand's butter quota allocation. Martin said the challenge smacked of a non-tariff trade barrier. The board had taken the matter to the European Commission. Page 1.

Labour leader Helen Clark said on Thursday she was prepared for coalition talks to continue into the Christmas holidays, saying she had underestimated how long they would take. Clark said if there was no clear indication by the end of the month from NZ First on whether they preferred to go into coalition

with National or Labour then "we're into longer term scenarios". Meanwhile, NZ First MP John Delamere said he expected his party would have a clearer idea in a couple of weeks whether it preferred National or Labour. Page 2.
Tertiary funding for 1997 is $1.13 billion - up almost one percent or $10.8 million - with nearly half the extra equivalent full-time student places allocated for teacher training. Page 2.

Carter Holt Harvey is cautiously optimistic that better times are ahead after reporting a 56 percent fall in tax-paid profit to $118 million for the half-year to September 30. The company believes it has now weathered the lows in the price cycle for most of its products. The result was in line with market expectations. Page 14.

The first three months of the new financial year have been "below expectations" for rural services company Wrightson, chairman Sir Ronald Trotter says. The company suffered below-budget performance in retail and real estate operations.

Speaking to the company annual meeting in Wellington on Thursday, Trotter said the full-year profit was likely to be at the lower end of the earlier forecast full-year profit range of $24 million to $27 million. Page 14.

Telecom Corporation said on Thursday its board was due to discuss the possibility of a share repurchase programme at a meeting next Thursday. Telecom also said it had made enquiries of its major shareholders, Bell Atlantic and Ameritech, about a news story on the possibility of one or both selling some or all of their shares. It said Bell Atlantic Enterprises International

vice president and chief financial officer Dermott Murphy said Bell Atlantic had a policy of "not communicating on any acquisition or disposition...unless there was unusual trading activity". Ameritech's treasurer and Telcom board member Rich Pehlke said he was "unaware of any such plans". Page 14.

Many people are impressed with the "massive and rapid" economic changes New Zealand has carried out, but they are not so impressed with the end result, Tradenz strategic development manager David Espie says. Page 15.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Labour will move a no-confidence motion challenging National's mandate to govern as a minority caretaker government if coalition talks are still deadlocked when Parliament resumes next month. But it seems such a motion would be defeated because it is unlikely to be endorsed by NZ First. That party does not appear to want any confidence motions while negotiations continue. Labour leader Helen Clark said on Thursday she would not be putting the motion to force NZ First's hand on coalition negotiations. Instead, Labour wants to prevent National entrenching itself in government over summer.

Telecom is expected to unveil plans for a share buyback involving up to $1.5 billion when it announces its half-year profit next Thursday. Depending on its capital requirements, the buyback could be done at once or over several years. It is understood the company has already been given the all-clear from its bankers for a buyback. Speculation about a buyback caused a sharp spike in Telecom's share price on Thursday, which finished up 16 cents at a record 762 cents on aggressive buying.
Fishing company Sanford has announced a one-for-10 bonus share issue after reporting a 14.1 percent lower tax-paid profit of $25 million for the August year.
Sales for the October first quarter at supermarket operator Progressive Enterprises fell by 0.5 percent, reflecting a poor performance from Georgie Pie and the Rattrays grocery wholesale business.
